paragraphs.text: This is [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition), the [oolong](oolong:definition) that shares its name with the cultivar it is made from, grown in [Anxi](anxi:where-it-is), a county of hills and ridges in southern Fujian, inland from Xiamen. The leaf was rolled into tight balls by [wrapping it in cloth](tieguanyin:making), pressing it and drying it a little, again and again, each round drawing it tighter. It was made in 1990, just as the [Tieguanyin boom](anxi:history) was about to change a county that had been among the poorer in the province.

At thirty-six years it falls in the third kind the trade sorts Tieguanyin into, [chenxiang, or old Tie](tieguanyin:styles): tea kept for years, not drunk fresh. The [light style](tieguanyin:ageing) goes stale quickly, so the heavier roasted kind is the one usually put away, and it is rested until the fire of the roast has settled.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
